rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, Tables 2-3, Figs 6-8 - laboratory column experiments on compacted silty sand amended with water hyacinth biochar, commercial mesquite biochar and coir pith, measuring SWRC, infiltration rate with a mini-disk infiltrometer and desiccation crack intensity.
rows.notes: The study has nothing to do with drip or sprinkler irrigation, crop yield or water productivity. It is a geotechnical laboratory study of biochar type effects on water retention, infiltration and desiccation cracking of a compacted silty sand intended for landfill covers and bioengineered slopes; no crops were grown and no irrigation method was compared. Only a passing remark in the discussion/conclusions suggests higher water retention could reduce irrigation demand for vegetation, which is speculation, not a result. The review's claim appears to be a misattribution to this study.

notes: Full text appears complete. The cited study (Hussain et al. 2020, Biochar 2:465-478) concerns biochar amendment of compacted soil, not irrigation technologies; the claim about drip versus sprinkler irrigation effects on yield and water productivity is not supported by any result in this paper.
